quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Relational Thinking and SELECT
quizzes.intro: Check tables, keys, filtering, and NULL basics before aggregation and joins.

questions.prompt: What is the best first question before writing a SQL query?

options.text: Which chart colors look nicest?
What should one row of the result represent (the grain)?
How can I use SELECT * in production?
Which table has the most columns?

questions.explanation: Grain defines the meaning of each result row and guides filters, joins, and aggregates.

wrongExplanations.a: Presentation comes after a correct logical result.
wrongExplanations.c: SELECT * is for exploration, not careful production reports.
wrongExplanations.d: Column count does not define the analytical question.

questions.prompt: Which statement about keys is correct?

options.text: A foreign key uniquely identifies a row in its own table only
A primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key points to a row in another table
Primary and foreign keys are interchangeable labels with no join impact
Keys are only used for chart titles

questions.explanation: Primary keys identify rows; foreign keys encode relationships used in joins.

wrongExplanations.a: That describes a primary key, not a foreign key.
wrongExplanations.c: Key roles are different and critical to correct joins.

questions.prompt: Which filter correctly finds rows where email is missing?

options.text: WHERE email = NULL
WHERE email IS NULL
WHERE email == None
WHERE email IS MISSING

questions.explanation: SQL tests missing values with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, not ordinary equality.

wrongExplanations.a: Equality with NULL does not behave as beginners expect.
wrongExplanations.c: That is not SQL null syntax.
wrongExplanations.d: IS MISSING is not standard SQL for this check.

questions.prompt: Why is a half-open date range often safer for month filters?

options.text: Because SQL cannot compare dates
Because >= start and < next month handles timestamps more reliably than naive BETWEEN end-of-month bounds
Because ORDER BY requires it
Because joins forbid BETWEEN

questions.explanation: Half-open intervals avoid missing or double-counting timestamped events around day boundaries.

wrongExplanations.c: Sorting is independent of this filtering pattern.
wrongExplanations.d: BETWEEN can be used, but must be handled carefully with timestamps.

questions.prompt: When mixing AND and OR in WHERE, what should you do?

options.text: Rely on memory of precedence and never use parentheses
Use parentheses to make intended grouping explicit
Replace all filters with SELECT *
Put OR conditions only in ORDER BY

questions.explanation: Parentheses prevent logic mistakes when combining AND and OR.

wrongExplanations.a: Implicit precedence is easy to misread and misuse.
wrongExplanations.c: SELECT * does not fix predicate logic.
wrongExplanations.d: ORDER BY sorts; it does not replace WHERE logic.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Aggregation and CASE
quizzes.intro: Test GROUP BY, HAVING, aggregates, and conditional logic.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between WHERE and HAVING?

options.text: WHERE filters groups; HAVING filters rows before grouping
WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
They are exact synonyms in all databases
HAVING can only be used with SELECT *

questions.explanation: WHERE restricts source rows; HAVING restricts aggregated groups.

wrongExplanations.c: They operate at different stages of query logic.
wrongExplanations.d: HAVING is unrelated to requiring SELECT *.

questions.prompt: Which aggregate counts unique customers correctly?

options.text: COUNT(*)
COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
SUM(customer_id)
AVG(customer_id)

questions.explanation: COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts unique values of the chosen key.

wrongExplanations.c: Summing IDs is not a customer count.
wrongExplanations.d: Averaging IDs is meaningless for counting customers.

questions.prompt: In standard SQL, if you SELECT region and SUM(total_amount), what else is required?

options.text: GROUP BY region
ORDER BY only
LIMIT 1 only
UNION ALL

questions.explanation: Non-aggregated selected columns must be included in GROUP BY in standard SQL.

wrongExplanations.b: ORDER BY sorts results; it does not define groups.
wrongExplanations.c: LIMIT restricts output size, not grouping correctness.
wrongExplanations.d: UNION ALL stacks result sets; it is not the grouping rule.

questions.prompt: What does CASE do in a SELECT list?

options.text: Deletes rows from the table permanently
Returns different values based on conditional logic
Creates indexes automatically
Forces every column to become text

questions.explanation: CASE encodes conditional business rules into calculated fields.

wrongExplanations.a: SELECT CASE does not delete data.
wrongExplanations.c: Indexes are schema objects, not CASE outputs.
wrongExplanations.d: CASE return types depend on the expressions you write.

questions.prompt: Why can averaging deal-level take rates misstate company take rate?

options.text: Because SQL cannot divide
Because unequal deal sizes mean a weighted ratio of totals is usually required
Because take rate is never a ratio
Because GROUP BY forbids ratios

questions.explanation: Aggregate numerators and denominators first, then divide, for blended rates.

wrongExplanations.c: Take rate is typically fees divided by GMV.
wrongExplanations.d: GROUP BY can support ratio calculations after sums.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Joins, Pitfalls, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Apply join thinking, fan-out awareness, and analytical judgment.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer a LEFT JOIN from customers to orders?

options.text: When you only want customers who definitely have matching orders
When you want all customers, including those with no orders
When you want to delete unmatched customers
When primary keys are optional

questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all left-side rows and fills nulls where the right side has no match.

wrongExplanations.a: That scenario usually calls for an INNER JOIN.
wrongExplanations.c: Joins do not delete customers from the source table.
wrongExplanations.d: Keys remain essential for correct matching.

options.text: A chart formatting style
Row multiplication from joining to a one-to-many relationship, which can inflate sums
A type of index
A mandatory ORDER BY clause

questions.explanation: Fan-out repeats left-side measures once per matching right-side row and can overstate totals.

wrongExplanations.a: Fan-out is a data logic issue, not a chart style.
wrongExplanations.c: Indexes affect performance, not this definition.

questions.prompt: After joining orders to payments, revenue suddenly triples. What should you do first?

options.text: Publish the dashboard immediately
Check whether the join multiplied order rows and aggregate to the correct grain before summing
Replace all joins with SELECT *
Assume the business tripled overnight

questions.explanation: Sudden magnitude shifts after joins often indicate grain breakage from fan-out.

wrongExplanations.a: Publishing without diagnosis risks major error.
wrongExplanations.c: SELECT * does not fix grain problems.

questions.prompt: Why are CTEs useful for beginners and teams?

options.text: They make queries impossible to audit
They stage readable intermediate logic such as filter, then join, then aggregate
They replace the need for WHERE
They automatically fix wrong keys

questions.explanation: CTEs improve clarity by naming steps, which makes review and debugging easier.

wrongExplanations.c: You still need predicates where appropriate.
wrongExplanations.d: Wrong keys must be fixed intentionally.

questions.prompt: Which habit best improves SQL trustworthiness?

options.text: Never check row counts
Define grain, test in layers, and reconcile key totals before presenting
Hide definitions so nobody questions them
Prefer the longest possible single-line query

questions.explanation: Trustworthy SQL is deliberate: clear grain, staged testing, and reconciliation.

wrongExplanations.a: Row counts catch fan-out and filter mistakes.
wrongExplanations.c: Hidden definitions create confusion and conflict.

questions.prompt: A query runs without error. What does that guarantee?

options.text: The business metric is correct
Only that the database could execute the statement—not that the logic matches the question
All joins were one-to-one
Nulls were handled correctly

questions.explanation: Execution success is necessary but not sufficient for analytical correctness.

wrongExplanations.c: Engines do not require joins to be one-to-one.
wrongExplanations.d: Null handling must be validated separately.
